Modern computing architecture rests on a hierarchy of abstractions. At the hardware level, transistors (currently fabricated at process nodes as small as three nanometers) perform binary logic operations. These are organized into functional units (arithmetic logic units, control units, cache memory) that collectively constitute a processor. The software stack above this hardware is layered: firmware, operating system kernel, system libraries, and application code.

Moore's Law (more accurately described as an observation rather than a physical law) predicted the doubling of transistor density approximately every two years. This trend held remarkably well from 1965 through roughly 2015, but has since decelerated due to fundamental physical constraints, including quantum tunneling effects at sub-five-nanometer scales.

Network architecture follows the OSI model (or, in practice, the more streamlined TCP/IP model), which separates communication functions into distinct layers. This separation of concerns enables independent development of protocols at each layer. The practical consequence is that an application developer need not understand radio frequency engineering to build software that communicates wirelessly.
